name: Medial epicanthoplasty

lead: Medial epicanthoplasty reduces or removes the epicanthal fold, the skin fold covering the inner corner of the eye. People use it to expose more of the inner corner, lengthen the eye's horizontal opening and change how wide-set the eyes look.

The fold is common in East Asian populations, and the operation is described mainly in Asian blepharoplasty, where it is often combined with double eyelid surgery. Evidence consists of retrospective series, an anatomical study and small trials. On looksmax.org users have discussed it for inner-corner shape, including planning surgery in Korea.

paras: Several techniques exist, including Z-plasty, Y-V advancement and skin-redraping methods, each rearranging skin at the inner corner to release the fold. It is frequently done in the same session as double eyelid surgery. The final look appears after swelling and scar maturation.
Scarring at the inner corner is the central concern; a randomised split-face trial tested botulinum toxin to reduce hypertrophic scars after the operation. Recurrence and asymmetry are also reported.

chain: Eye opens at the inner corner
angle.text: Medial epicanthoplasty releases the fold over the inner eye corner so the eye opens up and looks wider. The change is visible once healed and is often paired with double eyelid surgery. It is well described in the Asian blepharoplasty literature, mostly as case series.

lead: Medial epicanthoplasty is a cosmetic and reconstructive operation that reduces or removes the epicanthal fold, a vertical skin fold that partially covers the inner corner of the eye. People who have it describe the aim as showing more of the inner eye, lengthening the eye horizontally and, in some cases, changing how far apart the eyes look. The fold is particularly common in East Asian populations, where it frequently coexists with a missing upper eyelid crease [1][2].

The operation is reported mainly in the context of Asian blepharoplasty, where it is frequently combined with creation of a double eyelid fold. Surgeons in published series describe the aim as exposing more of the medial canthus and lengthening the eye's horizontal dimension [1][3][4]. A 2023 review of Asian upper blepharoplasty lists medial epicanthoplasty as a step surgeons add when needed to improve the cosmetic result [5].

Many techniques have been published, including Z-plasty and its variants, Y-V advancement, excision, skin redraping and root Z-epicanthoplasty. A 2016 systematic review of 46 articles found Z-plasty the most common approach, with redraping rising after 2007 [6]. Reported evidence consists of retrospective series, an anatomical study, small randomised trials on scar prevention and registered trials, and scarring at the inner corner is the recurring concern [3][7][8][9][10].

paras: The epicanthal fold is classified into types by origin; Wikipedia lists supraciliaris, palpebralis, tarsalis and inversus forms, and describes tarsalis as the type most often seen in East Asians [2]. It reports that the fold results mainly from enlargement of the preseptal part of the orbicularis oculi muscle, and that it is found in many populations, including near-universally in Japan and South Korea, with lower frequency in Europeans [2]. The same article notes that the fold is also associated with some medical conditions such as Down syndrome, and that it is often confused with the monolid: the monolid lacks an upper eyelid crease, while the fold covers the inner corner [2]. Wikipedia's epicanthoplasty page makes the same distinction, stating a person can have the fold, a crease, both or neither, and notes the fold overlies the tear drainage canals, which makes the operation challenging [11].

A 475-patient Korean American series described type 2 and type 3 folds as present in the majority of the East Asian population [7]. An anatomical and histological study examined the structure of the fold [12]. A 2016 review in Current Opinion in Ophthalmology describes the fold as made up of the preseptal part of the orbicularis oculi and says success depends on releasing vertical tension through subcutaneous dissection and orbicularis myectomy rather than flap design alone; it recommends discussing the fold and correction options with patients before upper eyelid surgery [13]. Some surgeons have argued that technique selection should depend on anatomical variation [14].

Surgeons group the many published approaches by how skin is rearranged at the inner corner. Z-epicanthoplasty and its modifications are among the best-known approaches [1][7][4]. The Y-V advancement technique was reported in 148 cases from 1989 to 1997 [8], and a skin-redraping method was reported in a series from 2002 to 2004 with the aim of lessening scarring and design complexity [3]. A comparison of three epicanthoplasty types has also been published, and combined epicanthoplasty with double eyelid surgery has been described for Chinese eyelids [15][16].

Park Z-epicanthoplasty, described by Jung and Min Park in 2007, places the incision within the eyelid skin rather than beside it; the authors say it is most useful for type III folds, is widely used for type II, and suits patients who want higher or outer-parallel double eyelid folds [17]. The 2016 systematic review by Hwang and Kim found that most literature addresses fold removal, only three articles covered reconstruction after removal, and that over-correction has led to published reconstruction methods [6]. The 2016 Saonanon review contrasts advancement and transposition flaps and says newer methods use shorter incisions, smaller flaps and less medial canthal ligament plication than older ones that left visible scars, under-correction or recurrence [13].

Authors repeatedly describe scarring at the medial canthus as an obstacle to be overcome [3][8], and surgeons have written that epicanthoplasty is sometimes avoided in Asian eyelid surgery because of the risk of noticeable scars [17]. Reported drawbacks also include under- or over-correction, asymmetry and recurrence [13][6]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, lists the same categories of risk [18]. Wikipedia notes that a Z-plasty is a common technique for correcting visible scar lines after epicanthoplasty [11].

Scar prevention has been tested in randomised trials. A split-face, double-blind trial of 43 patients who had Park Z-epicanthoplasty (30 completed) injected botulinum toxin type A on one side about a week after surgery and saline on the other; the toxin side had better Vancouver Scar Scale scores at 1, 3 and 6 months and about 87 percent of patients were satisfied overall [9]. A separate randomised trial of 70 Z-epicanthoplasty patients compared early 1540 nm non-ablative fractional laser plus silicone with silicone alone and reported better scar scores and satisfaction at six months in the laser group [10]. Another split-face trial of botulinum toxin is also published [19].

Surgeons writing in the 1990s described the epicanthal fold as an element of traditional Asian beauty that many patients nonetheless sought to reduce, particularly when combined with a double-eyelid procedure [1]. Grokipedia also notes debate over whether such surgery reflects Western ideals [18]. A 2014 T Nation thread shows the same debate, with one poster arguing that reducing the fold has no more to do with wanting to look white than a fake tan has to do with wanting to look black [20]. South Korea is widely described as a centre for this surgery, and a looksmax.org poster cites its surgeons' experience as the reason for choosing it [21].
Epicanthoplasty also has non-cosmetic roles: reconstructing or correcting folds associated with congenital conditions, and repair after trauma, are described in the surgical literature [2][6].

Looksmaxxing communities focus on the eye area, particularly eye spacing and the inner-corner shape. On looksmax.org, one user of Chinese/Kazakh background described having 'mongolic folds' and a perceived 5 to 6 mm deficit in ideal eye distance, and asked about having epicanthoplasty in South Korea, how to conceal post-operative marks, and budget; the poster also asked about softmaxxing procedures to add while abroad [21]. The post illustrates the way the procedure is discussed as a means of altering inner-eye spacing, combined with travel logistics and recovery planning.
Wikipedia's overview of looksmaxxing places surgical procedures within hardmaxxing, the category reserved for invasive methods [22].

Evidence includes retrospective surgical series of Z-plasty variants, Y-V advancement and skin redraping [1][3][7][8][4], a systematic review of 46 articles on epicanthoplasty methods [6], and randomised trials on scar prevention: botulinum toxin type A in a split-face design [9] and early fractional laser with silicone [10]. A second botulinum toxin trial is also published [19].

Registered trials include a completed 14-participant study of epicanthoplasty and upper-eyelid appearance (NCT06363422) [23] and a Phase 3 botulinum toxin study with 42 participants (NCT03294382) [24]. Most reported outcomes are surgeon-assessed or scar-scale scores, with fewer patient-reported measures of eye appearance.

lore.intro: Forum discussion is sparse; a looksmax.org thread shows epicanthoplasty being weighed as a way to change inner-corner shape and eye spacing, alongside travel and recovery logistics.[21]

claims.claim: Epicanthoplasty can correct a narrow-looking eye spacing caused by 'mongolic folds'.
Post-surgical marks can be hidden with makeup within a few weeks.
Epicanthoplasty is done well in South Korea, which is why people travel there for it.
The procedure can be combined with other eye work for a larger change in eye shape.
Scar prevention after surgery can be improved with early treatment.

timeline.event: W-epicanthoplasty is described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery [25].
Z-epicanthoplasty is described in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery [26].
Z-epicanthoplasty in Asian eyelids is published [1].
Modified Y-V advancement epicanthoplasty is reported [8].
Modified Z-epicanthoplasty in the Asian eyelid is reported in Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery [7].
Root Z-epicanthoplasty in Asian eyelids is published [4].
A skin-redraping medial epicanthoplasty is described, and Park Z-epicanthoplasty is published [3][17].
Medial epicanthoplasty based on anatomic variations is reported [14].
An anatomical and histological study of the epicanthal fold and a systematic review of epicanthoplasty methods are published [12][6].
A split-face randomised trial reports botulinum toxin for scar prevention after epicanthoplasty [9].
A randomised trial reports early fractional laser plus silicone for post-epicanthoplasty scars [10].
A 14-participant trial on epicanthoplasty and upper-eyelid appearance (NCT06363422) is registered as completed [23].
